title: AI Can Now Do 21% of Real Freelance Jobs, Up From 2.5% Last October. Will AI Take Your Job?
description:
A benchmark of 240 real projects, mostly paid freelance jobs, shows the best AI going from 2.5% to 20.83% of projects done at a quality a client would accept, in eleven months. This video explains what that test measures, why companies are cutting people anyway, and how to test your own job, task by task.

The numbers come from the Remote Labor Index by Scale AI and the Center for AI Safety, its public leaderboard as read on 2026-09-28, and the August 2026 job-cuts report from Challenger, Gray & Christmas. The task-by-task reading of a real job description is the channel owner's personal opinion, and the video labels it as such. Nothing here is career or financial advice.

Task list: information from O*NET OnLine by the U.S. Department of Labor, Employment and Training Administration (USDOL/ETA), used under the CC BY 4.0 license (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). O*NET® is a trademark of USDOL/ETA. The task statements in this video are shortened and translated into Chinese; USDOL/ETA has not approved, endorsed, or tested these modifications.

Recorded 2026-09-28.

chapters.hook: AI fails 96% of jobs? That number changed
chapters.test: What the Remote Labor Index measures
chapters.curve: The curve: 2.5% to 21% in eleven months
chapters.layoffs: So why do companies still cite AI for layoffs?
chapters.three-questions: Test your own job in three questions
chapters.outro: So will AI take your job?

eqsu.text: In February, one widely shared video said AI fails at ninety-six percent of real jobs. It was right, at the time.

z8yk.text: The same test now says the best AI finishes about twenty-one percent of real paid projects. Last October, it was two and a half.

md86.text: Here's what that test measures, why companies are cutting people anyway, and three questions that tell you what it means for your job.

xjp3.text: The test is called the Remote Labor Index. Scale AI and the Center for AI Safety built it.

nsjk.text: They collected two hundred forty real projects, most of them paid freelance jobs, across twenty-three kinds of work.

hkyj.text: Each AI gets the same brief and the same files the freelancer got.

mafu.text: Then human judges ask one question: is this as good as the professional's work, good enough that a client would accept it?

h865.text: These aren't toy tasks. There are two hundred forty of them.

qarp.text: The median project took a professional about eleven and a half hours. The median value was about two hundred dollars.

dr78.text: Together, the projects were worth about one hundred forty-four thousand dollars.

x4it.text: The automation rate is simple: the share of projects where the AI's work was judged as good as the human's, or better.

raaw.text: Now the curve. At launch last October, the best system, an agent called Manus, finished two and a half percent.

cign.text: In February, the best score was three point seven five percent. That's where the ninety-six percent headline came from.

dgig.text: By July, Claude Fable 5 reached fifteen point eight percent, the Center for AI Safety reported.

pukd.text: And today the leaderboard shows GPT-6 Astra at twenty point eight three percent, with Claude Fable 5.1 close behind.

kdwz.text: That's more than eight times better in eleven months.

7yny.text: And it still means the best AI fails about four out of every five real projects. Both of those are true at once.

ygm7.text: Why does it fail? At launch, the researchers sorted the rejections, and one project could fail for more than one reason.

y6mx.text: Nearly half were simply below professional quality.

9zx8.text: About a third were incomplete or malformed.

2hih.text: About one in six had technical or file problems, and about one in seven didn't match across files.

ztcf.text: The July report shows where it's heading. Fable 5 made a 3D ring redesign, a flat animated ad, and floor plans with renders.

8vis.text: The researchers call the ring much better than earlier AI work, and still say none of those three would be accepted as finished work.

9j6u.text: And some jobs are still out of reach, like transcribing music or playtesting a real-time game.

htip.text: One more detail matters for your office. When the researchers let AI grade AI, the graders overrated the work.

uwbw.text: By about three times for GPT-5.5, and about two and a half times for Opus 4.8.

a8f7.text: My reading: if your company judges AI work by asking another AI, expect a rosier answer than a client would give.

fvxx.text: Now the other side. The firm Challenger, Gray & Christmas counts announced US job cuts and the reasons employers give.

98gw.text: January to August this year, employers cited AI for one hundred sixteen thousand, one hundred seventy-five cuts.

9s5c.text: That's about twenty-two percent of all announced cuts. AI was the top reason every month from March to July.

neb9.text: Then in August, AI fell to the fourth most cited reason, with three thousand, four hundred sixty-two cuts.

b7gr.text: One month isn't a trend, but it's worth watching.

hgvq.text: Here's how both can be true. A layoff announcement and a benchmark answer different questions.

g23i.text: An announcement says the company is reorganizing around AI, expects more from fewer people, or is moving money to AI.

i3ws.text: The benchmark asks whether AI can deliver a whole project a client would accept. Today, that's about one in five.

sg7d.text: My reading: companies don't wait for five in five.

6d9q.text: I think they cut where AI already speeds up the tasks, and keep fewer people to check the rest.

6baw.text: So here's how to read the chart for your own job. Don't ask whether AI can do your job. Ask it task by task.

cq7p.text: One: can AI draft this task into something you can open and inspect?

edqy.text: Two: who checks it? You, a colleague, or the client?

9mdx.text: Three: what does a wrong one cost? Cheap to fix, or expensive to undo?

fkh7.text: Let's try it on a real job description: the US Labor Department's official task list for market research analysts.

bevd.text: It lists thirteen tasks. Here are eight of them, with my reading of each. This is opinion, not a measurement.

2p9b.text: Reports, charts, customer data, competitor prices, industry trends: AI can draft all of these today, and you check them.

zb5d.text: Survey design and campaign measurement: a first draft, then real judgment from you.

ss53.text: Directing interviewers and presenting to management are people work. AI can write the slides, not stand up in the room.

udm6.text: So by my count, four of eight tasks are drafts AI can make today, two are first drafts at best, and two are people work.

g39p.text: None of the eight is safe to hand over unchecked. That's what a four-in-five failure rate feels like at a desk.

z3fe.text: Do this with your own job this week. Write down the ten tasks you do most.

8yi9.text: Ask the three questions of each one, and mark it: AI drafts, first draft at best, or people work.

bk7j.text: Then do it again in six months. The chart moved eightfold in eleven months, so I'd expect your list to move too.

rh8y.text: So, will AI take your job? My answer: it's taking tasks first, and faster than February's headline suggested.

njt2.text: My view: the valuable skill is telling good work from almost good work. That's the part the test still needs human judges for.

pxdi.text: Which task on your list changes first? Tell me in the comments.
